insight.title: Plants Broadcast Airborne Warnings to Protect Neighboring Leaves
insight.subtitle: When under attack by insects, plants release chemical plumes into the wind to alert nearby neighbors before pests arrive.

sections.text: When a caterpillar begins chewing on a sagebrush leaf, nearby untouched plants instantly begin filling their own leaves with bitter defensive toxins before a single pest ever reaches them.

The damaged plant releases invisible airborne chemical compounds into the wind. Surrounding plants absorb these subtle signals through their leaves and immediately prime their defenses, anticipating an incoming attack.

Without nerves or a central brain, the field operates an early-warning radar system. Communication travels passively along atmospheric currents, converting isolated plants into a synchronized defensive network.
The wind becomes a broadcast network for silent defense.
